marks.description: Four characters 'made in the Jingtai reign', cast in relief, incised or chiselled, usually on the base of cloisonné vessels; sometimes on a later base plate or on a wooden stand added in the Qing court.
marks.what_it_is: An apocryphal reign mark for the Ming Jingtai emperor (1450-1457). It became a by-word for fine cloisonné, which is why cloisonné is still called jingtailan (景泰藍), and it was added to pieces of many later dates.

marks.notes: The four- and six-character forms are treated together by the sources; see cloisonne-da-ming-jingtai-nianzhi for the six-character form and the Qianlong 'two dragons' frame.

marks.description: Three characters, usually in iron-red seal script, on the base of enamelled glass (and some porcelain) snuff bottles.
marks.what_it_is: A hall mark linked by modern sources to a pavilion completed in 1767 in the Qianlong emperor's retirement quarters, for which enamel-on-glass wares were ordered; an older story (Bushell) made it the studio name of a glassmaker named Hu.
marks.dating_value: Genuine court pieces date to the later Qianlong reign; the mark was widely used on later enamelled glass and porcelain, so it alone proves nothing.
marks.later_copies: Republican and 20th-century enamelled milk-glass bottles with the mark are common (dealer attributions); Fitzwilliam dates its examples broadly 1750-1850.

marks.description: Inside-painted inscriptions usually give a two-character cyclical year (e.g. 丙申 bingshen), a month and often a place ('painted in the capital'), followed by the signature and seal.

marks.dating_value: A Shen family name places a piece in Fuzhou, most surviving examples late 19th-20th century; the sources used do not separate the 蘭記 and 恂記 branches.
marks.later_copies: Not documented by the sources used.

marks.description: Ryukyuan lacquer uses relief of lacquer putty (tsuikin), thin turban-shell mother-of-pearl and sub-tropical motifs; some Ryukyuan pieces carry Chinese inscriptions and dates.
marks.what_it_is: A convention: Ryukyu (Okinawa) made lacquer for tribute and export to China and Japan, and some pieces were inscribed in Chinese so as to pass as Chinese.
marks.dating_value: A Chinese inscription or date does not make a piece Chinese; scientific analysis can help separate regional lacquers.
marks.notes: Wikipedia is used for facts only; a museum source would be better (Okinawa Prefectural Museum, Urasoe Art Museum).
